text: Ms. Johnson, a seasoned high school teacher, had been dodging her classes for weeks by claiming a mysterious "family emergency," and the students knew exactly why - she was secretly running their bingo game every time they got a sub. Today's special guest was Mr. Thompson, who promptly brought in donuts for everyone and effortlessly called each student by name, much to the class's dismay. As he began his lesson plan, whispers started spreading: "free space energy, we're all doomed." Just as someone marked off the square "can't pronounce a single name," the door burst open and a stern-looking woman stormed in, introducing herself as Ms. Thompson, Mr. Thompson's cousin - an AP from the school district. But to everyone's surprise, she dropped her tough demeanor and announced that she'd been sent not to bust their bingo game, but to investigate the rumors of it, and was now eager to join in on the fun. As she marked off "brings snacks," the class erupted into cheers, welcoming their new ally in the most unlikely way possible.

text: Every time a new sub walked into the classroom, a hush fell over the room as the students frantically scanned their bingo cards, waiting for the chaos to begin. But today was different - the substitute, Mrs. Thompson (or rather, Rachel, Aunt Mildred's cousin), looked familiar, and it wasn't until she started talking about fractions that Emma noticed the family resemblance: same eyes, same nose, same awkward smile. As she marked off three squares with a flourish, muttering under her breath about how it was all due to the free space energy building up in the room, Alex whispered to her, "I think I see where this is going..." and sure enough, Rachel revealed that she was there to investigate reports of a secret bingo game being run in class. But instead of shutting it down, Rachel grinned mischievously and said, "You know what? I've got some experience with this sort of thing myself. Why don't you let me join the game?" With a triumphant shout, Emma called out "Do the chicken dance!" which prompted Rachel to stand up and flail her arms wildly in front of the whole class, while the students cheered and laughed along with her.

text: It was a day of unyielding chaos - April 15th, 2003, would forever be etched in the annals of time as the Battle of Exam Day: Operation Fire Drill. In the trenches of Room 304, the enemy - time - was rapidly slipping away from our beleaguered students, their pens scratching out feeble answers on the Scantron sheets like desperate cries for help. And then, without warning, the sirens pierced the air, a piercing clarion call that shook the very foundations of learning: the fire drill had been sounded, sending the entire class into a state of pandemonium. Amidst the mayhem, one casualty stood out - poor Timmy Jenkins, who refused to relinquish his grip on the Scantron, bubbles still rising from the answer sheet like tiny, defiant flags in the face of overwhelming adversity: he had to be physically dragged outside, his cries of "I'll finish this!" echoing through the hallways. As we regrouped outside, our casualties tallied - lost time, abandoned answers, and one very frustrated teacher - we knew that this was a day we would never forget. And as we all nodded in agreement, our collective voice rose to a deafening crescendo: "That was, without a doubt, the single most stressful ten minutes of the entire semester."

text:
On that fateful day, Mrs. Johnson's beleaguered English class was summoned to a final exam that would test their mettle and determine their academic futures, with the fate of at least one student already emerging as a casualty of procrastination. As they gathered around their desks, pens poised and eyes scanning the pages like weary veterans surveying the battlefield ahead, a shrill alarm pierced the air, shattering the calm and claiming its first victim - a poor unsuspecting notebook that fell to the floor, a collateral casualty of the chaos. The lights flickered ominously, casting eerie shadows on the walls as the intercom's robotic voice boomed out its dire warning: "This is not a test... This is not a drill." Pandemonium reigned supreme as students leapt from their seats, knocking over chairs and scattering papers in all directions like leaves before a tempest, while Mrs. Johnson struggled to restore order amidst the mayhem. Amidst the chaos, one student - Timmy - stood out, refusing to stop bubbling answers on his Scantron despite the alarm's cacophony, his eyes fixed intently on the form as if he alone understood that this was a test of wills, not a drill; it wasn't until Mrs. Johnson physically picked him up and began walking him outside, still clutching the offending Scantron, that even Timmy was finally convinced to stop bubbling answers and join in the evacuation.

As they all eventually made their way back into the classroom - shaken but unscathed - Mrs. Johnson raised her voice above the lingering din of the alarm, asking for a show of hands: "Who among you felt that this ten-minute ordeal was the most stressful experience of our entire semester?" Every single hand in the room shot up, a unanimous declaration of solidarity amidst the chaos. The class collectively shook their heads, exchanging looks of amazement and horror at the sheer audacity of it all - 10 minutes of unadulterated stress that would be etched into their memories forever.

**Emma:** What are we even writing about?

**Jack:** Does anyone have any ideas?

**Ryan:** I think Alex's intro paragraph is just a distraction from our real topic.

**Alex:** Shh, don't tell them about the other drafts!

**[15 minutes pass without anyone typing]**

**Jack:** Okay, I've got it! Let's write about the history of dental hygiene in ancient civilizations!

**Ryan:** Yeah, that sounds interesting!

**Emma:** Wait, what happened to our essay about pineapple?

**Alex:** Oh, don't worry about it. Let's just move on.

**[10 minutes pass]**

**Jack:** I've finished writing! Here's my draft:

"The ancient Egyptians were pioneers in dental hygiene, using twigs and ground pumice stone to clean their teeth..."

**Ryan:** Nice work!

**Emma:** And here's mine:

"In the 18th century, the invention of toothbrushes revolutionized oral care, making it more accessible to the general population."

**Alex:** Okay, let me just add a few sentences...

**[5 minutes pass]**

**Emma:** Alex, what are you typing?

**Jack:** Yeah, is that even our essay anymore?

**Ryan:** Wait, where's the pineapple?

**Alex:** Don't worry about it. I've submitted it.

**[all four of them simultaneously type "submit"]**

**Jack:** We did it! Our essay is done!

**Emma:** But what if they ask us about pineapple?

**Ryan:** Too late for that.

**[the doc is submitted]**

**Alex:** Now let's go get some pizza.

text: I was completely lost in my own world, daydreaming about my summer vacation plans when I felt the teacher's cold stare. Just as she opened her mouth to call on me, I snapped back to reality and prepared for impact. My strategy, which had miraculously worked eleven times already this semester, kicked in - I would simply repeat the last word she said back as a question. "Did?" I stammered out, hoping it was correct. To my surprise, she seemed taken aback, so I followed suit: "Did?" and then again with a shrug: "Did?" But just when I thought I'd gotten away with it one more time, she asked the unthinkable - "What is your favorite subject in school today?"

text: I slumped back in my chair, letting out a contented sigh as I let my mind wander to who-knows-where, completely zoning out for the first time all semester. Mr. Johnson stood at the front of the classroom and called out, "Jake Wilson," but I didn't flinch, too lost in thought to respond. He asked me another question, "J-A-K-E," but my response was just a weak "Jake?" repeated back as a question - it was a strategy that had worked an astonishing eleven times this semester already, and I was starting to think I might actually get away with not learning anything all year.
